title: Can we draw the next shape in each sequence?
description: The five shape sequences of the book are redrawn in the mind, and the next shape of each is looked at. The first four can be drawn by adding to the last shape, but the speed bump shapes soon have too many tiny segments.
teaching_notes: One idea: say in words what changes from one shape to the next, then use that rule to draw the next shape. Watch for students who think every sequence can be drawn for ever.

source: Figure it Out Q2 (Math Talk), p.11
video_script.why: The child states the rule of each shape sequence in words, uses it to draw the next shape, and sees why the last sequence is hard to draw, using the method of the solved examples.
video_script.substitution: Five sequences of shapes are looked at, and the next shape of each is found.
video_script.anchor: five rows of shapes, each with an empty frame for the next shape
video_script.payoff_line: We can draw the next shape in the first four sequences, but the last one is very hard

final_answer.value: open ended; typical: polygons one more side; complete graphs K7 with 7 dots; stacked squares 6 by 6; stacked triangles 6 rows; {{NAME_2}} too tiny to draw by hand
final_answer.spoken: the first four can be drawn, the last one is very hard

names.{{NAME_2}}: shape sequence where every line segment is replaced by a speed bump

maths_rules: regular polygons: the next shape has one more side
complete graphs: add a new dot and join it to every dot before; K7 has 7 dots and 15 + 6 = 21 lines
stacked squares: add a row and a column, 5 by 5 becomes 6 by 6, 36 little squares
stacked triangles: add a new bottom row, 5 rows become 6 rows
{{NAME_2}}: every segment becomes four, 768 x 4 = 3072 segments, each very tiny
the question is open ended; any clear rule in the child's own words is acceptable
video_script.design: Five rows of shapes stand one under the other, each with an empty frame at the end. The rule of each row is written in a few words, and the frame is filled for the first four rows.
open_questions: The book question is open ended; a typical answer is shown.

narration: <bookmark mark='rule'/>Step one, look at the regular polygons. Each shape has one more side than the one before.

narration: <bookmark mark='rule'/>Step two, look at the complete graphs. We add a new dot and join it to every dot before.
<bookmark mark='draw'/>The seventh dot joins the six dots already there, so we can draw the next graph too.

beats.on_screen: Step 3: stacks: squares: add a row and a column, 5 by 5 becomes 6 by 6; triangles: add a new bottom row, 6 rows

narration: <bookmark mark='rule'/>Step four, look at the {{NAME_2}} shapes. Every segment is replaced by a speed bump.
<bookmark mark='many'/>The last shape has seven hundred sixty eight segments, and each one becomes four.
<bookmark mark='tiny'/>That is seven hundred sixty eight times four segments, and each one is very tiny.

beats.on_screen: Step 5: check a graph: 7 dots each joined to 6 others = 7 x 6 = 42 ends, 42 / 2 = 21 lines; 15 + 6 = 21

marks.ends: each of the seven dots is joined to six others, giving forty two line ends

narration: <bookmark mark='ends'/>Step five, check the graph with seven dots. Each dot joins six others, so there are forty two line ends.
<bookmark mark='half'/>Every line has two ends. Half of forty two gives twenty one, which matches fifteen plus six.

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>We can draw the next shape in the first four sequences, but the last one is very hard. <bookmark mark='tiny'/>Its next shape has three thousand seventy two segments, and they are tiny. <bookmark mark='rule'/>Each rule tells us what to add or replace in the shape before.
